summary: In late March and April 2026, South African social-grant beneficiaries were directed to complete SASSA eLife certification, including an online biometric route connected to other government systems. SASSA acknowledged that interface glitches prevented some notified beneficiaries from using the self-service portal, delayed certification, and produced office queues and transport burdens; it announced restoration on 10 April. Reporting on 23 April documented continuing facial-recognition, one-time-pin and Home Affairs interface failures, including pensioners who said 22 facial-scan attempts failed; SASSA acknowledged intermittent downtime while reporting most portal users verified successfully. In-person fingerprint verification existed but imposed travel and waiting. Separate quarterly figures report 67,868 grant suspensions from mixed noncompliance causes; they do not establish that this portal outage or an individual failed facial match caused a suspension.

primary_classification.classification_basis: Beneficiaries with valid or unresolved grant entitlement were blocked by an unavailable biometric verifier, while the office fallback imposed material travel and queue burdens.

assessment_boundaries: Agency claims of restoration conflict with later individual reports of intermittent failure; neither establishes universal access or a quantified outage duration.
Office fingerprint verification was available in principle but the directly reported travel and long queues materially burdened the alternative; adequacy for every affected beneficiary is unknown.
The 67,868 quarterly suspensions encompass multiple noncompliance causes and cannot be attributed to facial failure or the April outage.

An individual pensioner report now establishes a withheld-grant outcome alongside repeated biometric failure, but no public SASSA decision file or reason code shows that the unresolved biometric result itself supplied the authority for the initial suspension.
vigil_assessment.factual_basis: SASSA’s 10 April primary statement confirms that notified grant recipients could not access its self-service eLife certification portal because interfaces with other departments glitched; completion was delayed and office queues resulted. SASSA says people who must certify within a stipulated period may face payment delay or suspension if they do not complete the process, and may be interpreted as deceased or ineligible; this is a stated rule and potential consequence, not proof of a particular suspension caused by the outage. IOL’s 23 April reporting provides beneficiary accounts of repeated facial-scan failures (one couple said 22 tries), OTP errors and Home Affairs unavailability after the claimed restoration. A SASSA spokesperson said 13,644 of 15,499 unique online users were verified by 16 April and acknowledged intermittent downtime. Later parliamentary-answer reporting gives 67,868 quarterly suspensions across varied noncompliance causes and 7,779 electronic facial-system complaints, while SASSA said failed facial checks could be redirected to office fingerprint verification. These aggregates do not connect a particular failed facial result to a binding grant-suspension decision. The preserved eNCA card-migration article remains service context only, not occurrence proof.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: When interdependent verification was unavailable or inconclusive, the online certification pathway became practically inaccessible and the office route shifted cost and delay onto beneficiaries. That is an access-continuity failure with a bounded alternative, not proof that a biometric uncertainty state itself authorised a grant suspension. The agency’s potential suspension rule and the aggregate suspension count remain distinct from an observed individual decision.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: Essential-benefit verification needs a workable fallback when an identity service or interagency interface fails. Here SASSA’s own account confirms interruption and queues, while beneficiary reporting shows some problems persisted after announced restoration. The question of whether any specific grant was suspended because of a failed facial check requires decision-level evidence.

SASSA acknowledged interface glitches that delayed and disrupted completion of the eLife certification process, generated long queues and required affected beneficiaries to incur transport and waiting burdens until the self-service system was restored. This is material disruption of an important public-benefit access workflow with bounded recovery. Threshold applied: Material disruption of an important service or organisational workflow; a critical or important function unavailable for more than two hours; complete relevant cloud-service unavailability over 30 minutes; or limited availability affecting over five percent or one million EU users, whichever is smaller, for over one hour, with bounded recovery.
